messages.subject: Cormack-Jolly-Seber implementation
parts:
Dear Stan team,

I've enjoyed working with Stan, in part due to the effort the team puts into effective documentation and open discussion on these forums (thank you!). I have an implementation of the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model commonly used in wildlife studies to estimate survival in the context of mark-recapture experiments. I searched the Stan mailing list and the example models repo but only found an  "I'll try to implement this" email from a very busy person so I don't think an example is available so far. 

I am writing to share the implementation even though it's not clear to me if there's an easy way to make the model independent of the data-munging R code.   This version of the model strikes a balance between being simple enough to grasp and tackling some of the implementation issues that come up with any non-trivial data set.  Even with tens of thousands of observations the run time is  quick so I'm pretty confident the basic calculation is not doing anything terribly wrong efficiency-wise.  I am working on writing this code up more formally as part of an analysis but I don't think more complex models will make a good example.  If someone from the Stan team can provide some guidance and a little help in cleaning this up and simplifying it into a Stan example that's something I can put some time into.  The model consultation guide asks for a license to let's use the same one as the manual for this CJS example:  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/).

First a few things about the model:
  1. The model applies to a population of individuals
  2. Within a population individuals start out as un-tagged and un-modelled
  3. At discrete time points, an attempt is made to capture and tag individuals.
  4. After individuals are tagged they are available for recapture.
  5. The survival probability over an interval is traditionally called $\phi_{i,t}$, and the recapture probability is traditionally called $p_{i,t}$.  Both can be estimated from a record of captures and recaptures, though they do have to be constrained by an outside model.
  6. The data are in a row-oriented format.  I made this decision to avoid constructing an n_individuals x n_time_points matrix as in my large real data set time points are often individual specific (within bounds). 
  7. The tricky part was figuring out how to sum over possible states after the last recapture, this is the A/B/A_star/B_star loop in the cjs.stan model.  The implementation could be neater but this way is iterative and lets me avoid re-doing parts of the summation at each step.

To get the data in order, I classified each row (capture or recapture) using a sort-of self-evident R function.  Details:

  1. Possible states are 1-7,
  2. 'surviving == 1' means the individual is know to be alive (from first observation to last observation, inclusive of the observations). 
  3. Once 'surviving == 0' the Stan model sums over possible states.  
  4. 'boundary_detection' means we detected an individual at the site boundary and never again (proxy for emigration).
  5. 'trap_recapture' means we detected an individual (salmon!) in a smolt trap (another kind of emigration).
  6. 'season_break' rows exist because different covariates apply before and after the row (but there is not capture).
  7. In a very basic cjs model this classification could just be recaptured/uncaptured/not_seen_again.

cjs_classification = function(status, surviving, censored, tagged) {
    cjs_classification <- vector(mode='numeric', length=length(status))
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 1 & status == 'recaptured'] <- 1
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 1 & status == 'uncaptured'] <- 2
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 1 & status == 'boundary_detection'] <- 3
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 1 & status == 'trap_recapture'] <- 4
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 1 & status == 'season_break'] <- 5
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 0 & censored == 0 &
                       (status == 'season_break' | status == 'uncaptured')] <- 6
    cjs_classification[tagged == 1 & surviving == 0 & censored == 1] <- 7
    return(cjs_classification)
  }

The basic Stan code is below (also attached in case I mangle it).  The 'interval' covariate is the time duration (in days) from row i-1 to row i.  I''m only giving the sketch of the data handling code here because it ends up being pretty data-set specific.  The semi-generic part of the code is in (https://github.com/sakrejda/westbrook-data).

data {
  int n_rows;
  int n_censored;
  int n_ambiguous_individuals;

  int n_unambiguous_rows;
  int n_ambiguous_rows;
  int n_individuals;
  int ambiguous_rows[n_ambiguous_individuals,2];
  int unambiguous_rows[n_unambiguous_rows];

  vector[n_rows] interval;
  int season[n_rows];
  int cjs_classification[n_rows];
}

transformed data {
  int ambig_row_calc_buffer;
  int m;

  ambig_row_calc_buffer <- 0;
  for ( i in 1:n_ambiguous_individuals ) {
    m <- ambiguous_rows[i,2] - ambiguous_rows[i,1] + 1;
    if ( m > ambig_row_calc_buffer ) {
      ambig_row_calc_buffer <- m;
    }
  }
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> phi_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> p_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha_seasonal[4];
  real<lower=0, upper=1> rho_seasonal[4];
}

model {
  real row_lp[n_rows];
  int k;
  int start_row;
  int stop_row;
  real A[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real A_star[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real B[ambig_row_calc_buffer];
  real B_star[ambig_row_calc_buffer];

  vector[n_rows] phi;
  vector[n_rows] p;
  vector[n_rows] alpha;
  vector[n_rows] rho;

  for ( i in 1:4 ) {
    phi_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,5);
    p_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,5);
    alpha_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,25);
    rho_seasonal[i] ~ beta(5,25);
  }

  for ( i in 1:n_rows ) {
    phi[i] <- pow(phi_seasonal[season[i]],interval[i]*(4/365.25));
    p[i] <- p_seasonal[season[i]];
    alpha[i] <- alpha_seasonal[season[i]];
    rho[i] <- rho_seasonal[season[i]];
  }                                                                                            
  for ( i in 1:n_unambiguous_rows ) {
    k <- unambiguous_rows[i];
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 0) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated.");
      row_lp[k] <- 0.0;
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 1) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k])*p[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 2) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k])*(1-p[k]));
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 3) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*rho[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 4) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*rho[k]*alpha[k]);
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 5) {
      row_lp[k] <- log(phi[k]*(1-rho[k])*(1-alpha[k]));
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 6) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated here.");
    }
    if (cjs_classification[k] == 7) {
      print("STOP, row ", k, " should not be evaluated.");
      row_lp[k] <- 0.0;
    }
    increment_log_prob(row_lp[k]);
  }

  for ( i in 1:(n_ambiguous_individuals)) {
    for ( j in 1:ambig_row_calc_buffer ) {
      A[j] <- 0.0;
      B[j] <- 0.0;
      A_star[j] <- 0.0;
      B_star[j] <- 0.0;
    }
    start_row <- ambiguous_rows[i,1];
    stop_row <- ambiguous_rows[i,2];
    for ( j in start_row:stop_row ) {
      k <- j - start_row + 1;
      if (cjs_classification[j] != 6) {
        print("STOP, row ", j, " should not be evaluated here.");
      }
      if (j == start_row) {
        A[k] <- 1.0;
        A_star[k] <- 1.0;
      } else {
        A[k] <- phi[j-1]*(1-p[j-1]);
      }
      B[k] <- (1-phi[j]);

      A_star[k] <- A_star[k] * A[k];
      B_star[k] <- A_star[k] * B[k];

    }
    increment_log_prob(log(sum(B_star)));
  }


}

With a rapidly expanding community, and an even faster growing list of features
to implement, helping users to understand and optimize their models is becoming
a bit overwhelming.  Of course we don’t want to limit the help we can provide and
so in an effort to reduce redundant answers and provide more resources to users
new to Stan we are hoping to formalize our consultation procedure.
 
Firstly, when asking a question please try to provide as much information as possible
and be specific with your issues.  
 
Providing a model with an init file and (pseudo)data, especially a simplified model that
manifests the pathology you are seeing, is the best way to provide context to your
question.  Also please be aware that not everyone uses the same interfaces, and
so providing your model in as many formats as possible will significantly improve
the probability of a prompt response (currently many devs use CmdStan, and Rstan
provides various functions for outputting data frames into compatible formats).
Also, please follow the style guidelines in the manual!  The easier it is for
someone to read your model the faster we’ll be able to respond.
 
Specificity is also critical.  Complaining of a “slow” model is extremely ambiguous,
whereas small ESS, large Rhat, and reduced ESS/time are much more informative
and allow us to identify possible issues immediately.  

Line search fails in optim at a late step.
 
Secondly, we would like go curate many of these questions into reference models
and provide new users a suite of illustrative examples in model building, validation,
and optimization.  Each entry will include a user summary of the problem and its
resolution, developer notes adding supporting information and references, and
(possibly simplified) models a user can run themselves.  
 
If you are interested in participating then please indicate as much as the beginning
of your question along with the open source license under which you would prefer the
discussion and any subsequent models to be released.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cormack-Jolly-Seber implementation

Thanks for sharing.

We only need licenses on things we're going to distribute.
And then code and doc are usually under separate kinds of licenses.

We actually have a bunch of implementations of CJS
that are going to get rolled into the new model repository.

Right now, they're loitering on a branch:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/feature/issue-451-mark-recapture-egs/src/models/misc/mark-recapture

The K-versions clean up the loops into something a big more
general that you might want to take a look at. Your version is
just unfolding it, which is fine.

Fränzi Korner-Nievergelt has implemented some more serious CJS
type models with covariates.

- Bob

> With a rapidly expanding community, and an even faster growing list of features
> to implement, helping users to understand and optimize their models is becoming
> a bit overwhelming. Of course we don’t want to limit the help we can provide and
> so in an effort to reduce redundant answers and provide more resources to users
> new to Stan we are hoping to formalize our consultation procedure.
>
> Firstly, when asking a question please try to provide as much information as possible
> and be specific with your issues.
>
> Providing a model with an init file and (pseudo)data, especially a simplified model that
> manifests the pathology you are seeing, is the best way to provide context to your
> question. Also please be aware that not everyone uses the same interfaces, and
> so providing your model in as many formats as possible will significantly improve
> the probability of a prompt response (currently many devs use CmdStan, and Rstan
> provides various functions for outputting data frames into compatible formats).
> Also, please follow the style guidelines in the manual! The easier it is for
> someone to read your model the faster we’ll be able to respond.
>
> Specificity is also critical. Complaining of a “slow” model is extremely ambiguous,
> whereas small ESS, large Rhat, and reduced ESS/time are much more informative
> and allow us to identify possible issues immediately.
>
> Line search fails in optim at a late step.

> Secondly, we would like go curate many of these questions into reference models
> and provide new users a suite of illustrative examples in model building, validation,
> and optimization. Each entry will include a user summary of the problem and its
> resolution, developer notes adding supporting information and references, and
> (possibly simplified) models a user can run themselves.
>
> If you are interested in participating then please indicate as much as the beginning
> of your question along with the open source license under which you would prefer the
> discussion and any subsequent models to be released.
